quote: But I maintain that she would come if we worked for her, and that so to work, even in poverty and obscurity, is worth while.
source: Virginia Woolf, A Room of One’s Own, chapter 6, the closing sentence (1929)
note: She is Shakespeare’s sister, the gifted poet Woolf imagines, who died young and never wrote a word. The wording and the citation stand as proposed; only this note naming her was added.

evidence.where: Project Gutenberg Australia HTML of A Room of One’s Own, fetched again with curl and the last paragraph read in place; the sentence is the final one of the text, directly before THE END, and the same paragraph names “the dead poet who was Shakespeare’s sister”
evidence.edition: A Room of One’s Own (Hogarth Press, 1929); Project Gutenberg Australia 0200791h
evidence.locator: Chapter 6, last sentence of the book, following “that we cannot expect, for that would be impossible.”

reason: Third independent reading finds the sentence word for word as the book’s last, “worth while” two words, in Woolf’s own voice; not shipped, Woolf 0 of 3, not banned. The refutation faulted only the bare pronoun, so the line ships with a note naming her; nothing in quote or source changed.
